beats.text: On the 24th of November, the Wikipedia page for Cristiano Ronaldo listed 987 official goals, for club and country combined. That leaves 13 to reach 1,000.
He is 41. This season, for Al-Nassr, he has scored 11 goals in 14 matches. So the question sounds easy. When does he get there, and how sure can we be?
This video asks something narrower than how hard 1,000 goals is. A date, with odds. I built a simple model from his own record, and I will show every assumption, including the parts it cannot see.
Here is the short version. If he keeps scoring like the last two seasons, the model puts the chance he has done it by late February at 41 percent, and by late May at 99 percent.

The first problem is that nobody agrees on the total. Wikipedia, in a revision from the 24th of November, says 987. A tracker called messixronaldo, updated on the 20th, says 986. Another, ronaldogoalscore, says 984 as of the 26th.

Look at the dates. The tracker with 986 is dated six days before the one with 984. So this is not one page being out of date. They count differently, and I could not tell from the pages themselves how.
The match counts differ too. 1,347 official appearances on Wikipedia, 1,342 on one tracker, 1,334 on the other.
Wikipedia splits its total into 841 goals for his clubs and 146 for Portugal. Add the two and you get 987.

I use the Wikipedia figure as the baseline, because it names a revision I can cite. Then I run the model again with the lowest figure, 984, as a check. That is 13 goals needed in one case, and 16 in the other.
Now the rate. These are his goals for clubs in each season. The best year was 2014 to 2015, with 61 goals in 54 matches.
That was at Real Madrid, and it works out at 1.13 goals a match. No other season of his is higher.
Plot the rate against his age and you can see it fall from the mid thirties. The lowest season since he turned 33 is 2022 to 2023, at 0.49 a match.
His first season at Juventus, 2018 to 2019, was 28 goals in 43 matches. That is 0.65 a match, well under what came before it.
Then Al-Nassr. 50 goals in 51 matches in 2023 to 2024. 35 in 41. 30 in 37. And this season, 11 in 14. The rate has eased, but it is still close to 0.8 a match.
I should say what the rate includes. It counts goals in all official matches. The table I used does not split out penalties, so neither does the model.
So how many matches does he need? At his club rate over the last two seasons, 0.83 goals a match, 13 goals is about 16 matches.

How long is that? In the last two seasons he averaged about four club matches a month, and Portugal added a little under one. So I assume about 4.7 matches a month. That assumes a ten month club season, which is my assumption, not a fact I fetched.
Turn it around. To get there in three months he needs 0.92 goals a match. In six months, 0.46. In twelve months, 0.23. Against recent seasons at around 0.8, only the three month target is a stretch.
That is why the rate matters less than you would think. Thirteen goals is so few that the number of matches he plays decides most of the answer.
Here is the model. Each line is the chance he has reached 1,000 by a date. First line: his last two seasons hold. By late January, 7 percent. By late February, 41. By late March, 77. By late May, 99.
On that line, the middle of the range is around the end of March 2027.
Second line: his rate keeps falling at the pace of the last three seasons, about 9 percent a year. It sits almost on top of the first. Same middle date.

Third line: his rate drops to 0.49 a match, his worst season since 33. Now the middle moves to the end of May. By late February the chance is 3 percent, by late May it is 61, and by a year from now it is 99.8.

Now the cautious check. Use the lowest count, so 16 goals are needed. The middle date slips a month in the falling case, and to the end of June in the sharp case. The chance by late May in the sharp case falls to 32 percent.
First, injuries. The model has none. A few weeks out and every date moves by those weeks.

Second, how long he keeps playing. I did not research his contract or any plans to retire, so the model assumes he plays on through the whole period. That could be wrong, and this video makes no claim about it.
Third, the fixture list. I assumed a steady number of matches a month. Real calendars have breaks, and matches come in clusters. I did not fetch his fixtures.
And I have no minutes and no penalty split, so the model treats every match as the same.
So treat the curve as arithmetic, not as a prediction about a man. Given his own record and these assumptions, 13 goals is a small number.
Here is where I land. If the Wikipedia count is right and he keeps playing, the middle of the range is late March 2027, with a spread from late February to the end of May.
Every figure here came from the pages named on screen and in the description, with the date I fetched them. The method and the output file are kept with this video.
One question for you. Which count would you trust, and what would you change in the model? Tell me in the comments.
